extracted.intended_audience: general readers of humorous travel writing; tourists and prospective travelers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and implied evaluative principles embedded in a 19th-century humorous travelogue about how to view art, behave as a tourist, and judge guides, museums, and local customs. Useful for readers and writers of satirical travel accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guide conduct — show and be silent
rubrics_metrics.description: A good guide should show a masterpiece, then step aside and hold still for at least ten minutes to let visitors think; constant chatter from guides is an anti-pattern that spoils the tourist experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrator criticizes guides who 'talk forever' and 'interrupt every dream, every pleasant train of thought, with their tiresome cackling.' Example admonition: 'If they would only show you a masterpiece ... and then step aside and hold still for ten minutes and let you think, it would not be so bad.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism toward guide-superlatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Be wary of guide claims and superlative descriptions of local 'wonders' — verify rather than accept inflated praise at face value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrator repeatedly finds advertised 'wonders' underwhelming (echo, painted arbor, amphitheatre-turned-race-track). He advises a healthy suspicion of extravagant guide talk and placard proclamations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for deterioration when evaluating artworks
rubrics_metrics.description: When judging old works, consider loss of color, scale and damaged expression; praise that treats decayed works as if they retain original attributes can be mistaken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discussion of da Vinci's Last Supper: colors 'dimmed with age,' 'countenances are scaled and marred,' yet visitors speak as if 'faultless drawing' and 'matchless coloring' remain. The narrator permits that a trained artist might mentally restore missing qualities, but ordinary admiration often projects vanished details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution interpreting 'expression' in painted faces
rubrics_metrics.description: Most people cannot reliably read or interpret what a painted face 'expresses'; assertions about expression are frequently subjective and contradictory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim that 'there is not one man in seventy-five hundred that can tell what a pictured face is intended to express' is illustrated by anecdotes where different critics read opposing emotions in the same work and an actor's comic demonstration of wildly varying readings of his own face.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand copies vs originals — copies may seem superior
rubrics_metrics.description: Copies and reproductions can appear more beautiful or 'handsome' than deteriorated originals; do not assume a copy's superiority invalidates the original's former greatness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrator notes that engravings and copies of the Last Supper often look better to him than the faded original; he suggests some admiration is for an imagined former state rather than present reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize nationality bias in artists' depiction of subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Old masters frequently painted figures in the likeness of their own nation; consider the painter's cultural perspective when assessing ethnic authenticity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation that Italian artists painted Italian Virgins, Dutch painters painted Dutch Virgins, etc., and that artists unconsciously 'worked his nationality into the picture' (example: allegorical copy where all soldiers look German).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical travel requirement — carry personal soap
rubrics_metrics.description: Travelers should carry their own soap because local hotels and public baths often do not supply it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated anecdotes about having to send out for soap and the narrator's conclusion that English travelers know better and bring soap with them; humorous episode with Blucher's broken French note demanding 'savon.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't rely uncritically on poorly translated signs or placards
rubrics_metrics.description: Printed explanatory cards, hotel advertisements, and museum placards frequently contain bad translations that can mislead or amuse; take their textual claims with a grain of salt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: hotel card headed 'NOTISH' with mangled English, and the placard describing figures in the Last Supper with awkward, misleading phrasing such as 'Bartholomew ... uncertain and doubtful about what he thinks to have heard.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Embrace local leisure customs — prioritize comfort when traveling
rubrics_metrics.description: Part of the charm of travel is adopting the local pace — repose, public promenading, evening music and moderate habits — rather than American hurry; relaxing is a legitimate travel aim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast between European customs of evening promenades, beer halls, band music and orderly leisure versus American restlessness; the narrator endorses occasional 'lay[ing] ourselves on the shelf' to renew energies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess relics and treasures in cultural context
rubrics_metrics.description: Extravagant church treasures and relic displays may be materially lavish yet serve a moral or didactic purpose (e.g., reminders of mortality); evaluate both the spectacle and its intended sermon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Description of Milan Cathedral's glittering relics and the 'pregnant sermon' of the decayed saint: 'You that worship the vanities of earth... behold their worth!' The narrator juxtaposes the show's gaudiness with the intended moral message.
